title: A Production-Grade, High-Efficiency Agentic RL Framework for Frontier LLMs with Validated Recipes

paper.title: A Production-Grade, High-Efficiency Agentic RL Framework for Frontier LLMs with Validated Recipes
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a critical phase in the post-training pipeline of large language models (LLMs). As the frontier of LLM capabilities shifts from static reasoning to agentic tasks—characterized by external tool invocation, multi-turn interactions, and long-horizon decision-making—existing mainstream RL frameworks have grown increasingly unwieldy, raising the overhead of adoption, usage, and debugging.
To address these challenges, we present LoongSage, an agent-native, fully asynchronous RL framework with a lightweight core of roughly 14K lines of code. Built upon Megatron for distributed training and SGLang for high-throughput inference, LoongSage centralizes orchestration within a single controller process and encapsulates all GPU-resident components as Ray actors. It introduces AgentFlow, a unified execution paradigm that orchestrates both white-box and black-box agents. For asynchronous execution, it integrates sliding-window strategies that bound trajectory staleness, and employs TransferMesh, a topology-aware synchronization mechanism that routes weights after each step over the fastest transport available to each receiver.
Beyond agentic RL, LoongSage incorporates a memory-efficient Teacher Manager that decouples the scaling of teacher models from GPU memory constraints, natively supporting Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation. Extensive evaluations across four complete training runs, spanning complex reinforcement learning and multi-teacher distillation, demonstrate that task rewards improve steadily while the train–inference gap is kept under continuous control, and the fully asynchronous pipeline removes synchronous idle bubbles, sustaining hardware utilization.

Historically, the GPT series leveraged Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) to translate human preferences into optimizable objectives, establishing the viability of instruction-following assistants ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) . More recently, models like DeepSeek-R1 have demonstrated that, given verifiable rewards, complex behaviors such as extended chain-of-thought reasoning, self-correction, and backtracking can emerge through RL optimization ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2022 ) . As the focus transitions from instruction following to complex reasoning, RL has shifted from a secondary fine-tuning step to a central phase for instilling core model capabilities. Despite these reasoning advancements, text generation alone is insufficient for executing complex, real-world projects. This limitation has catalyzed exploration into tool-calling capabilities ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Schick et al., 2023 ) , driving the paradigm shift towards agentic RL. In this context, reward signals are no longer confined to the correctness of single-turn responses. Instead, they evaluate an agent’s holistic ability to complete tasks by invoking tools, manipulating files, executing tests, and refining actions iteratively based on environmental feedback. Consequently, coding, research, and computer-use agents have established end-to-end task completion as a new capability frontier ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) . Compared to single-turn tasks, agentic RL unfolds over extended horizons with persistent multi-turn states, necessitates sandboxed execution for external side effects, and produces heavy-tailed episode distributions ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) . This fundamental shift redefines the role of an RL framework from merely generating and scoring text to continuously driving and recording a system operating within dynamic environments. However, many existing RL frameworks are rooted in assumptions inherited from single-turn RLHF or verifiable-reward workloads ( Hu et al., 2025 ) , rendering them suboptimal for agentic training. While some systems introduce controller-centered abstractions ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) or deliberately narrow the pairing of backend engines ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , none are architected natively for the complexities of agentic training, which directly translate into production overheads. For instance, memory constraints typically bottleneck the number of teachers in multi-teacher distillation, and synchronous train-inference loops suffer severe utilization drops due to long-tailed trajectory rollouts. Furthermore, several systemic discrepancies manifest as implicit off-policy drift: mismatches in tokenization, numerical precision, and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing between the training and inference engines. These are compounded by loose trajectory reconstruction—a subtle but accumulating divergence between the inference-generated sequences and the training-consumed data. Because algorithmic hyperparameters cannot tune away these systemic issues, a modern framework must elevate resource management, train-inference decoupling, numerical consistency, and trajectory fidelity to first-class design primitives. To address these critical gaps, we present LoongSage , a lightweight agentic RL training framework engineered for production-grade workloads. Built specifically upon Megatron ( Shoeybi et al., 2019 ) for distributed training and SGLang ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) for high-throughput inference, LoongSage encapsulates the most demanding and error-prone complexities of agentic RL within its architecture while maintaining a lightweight, extensible, and user-friendly core. Notably, we open-source not only the framework but also the validated training recipes, enabling researchers to initialize runs from configurations proven on frontier models rather than starting from scratch. Its key features include: • Seamless Integration of Any Agent: LoongSage accommodates any white-box or black-box agent via a standard chat-completions interface with zero intrusion into agent logic. Its AgentFlow paradigm maintains strict token-level alignment (Token-In, Token-Out; TITO), feeding the training engine the exact token streams generated during inference, thereby decoupling the framework core from domain-specific agent implementations. • Staleness-Bounded Fully Asynchronous Training: By decoupling the sampling and optimization phases via a train-rollout buffer, the fully asynchronous pipeline substantially improves hardware utilization. To strictly bound the resulting trajectory staleness, it employs sliding-window strategies, bringing off-policy drift under explicit control. • Topology-Aware Weight Synchronization: Through TransferMesh, LoongSage transfers weights from training to inference as a continuous named tensor stream. The system automatically selects the optimal transport layer—such as a CUDA IPC handle for colocated GPUs or an NCCL broadcast for distributed nodes—based on the physical device topology, keeping the synchronization process completely transparent to both backend engines. • Full-Vocabulary Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation: An independent Teacher Manager treats teacher models as dynamically managed compute resources, decoupling the permissible number of teachers from the student model’s GPU memory constraints to enable scalable multi-teacher distillation. Furthermore, it natively supports a composable, multi-paradigm objective function—spanning PG-style, GKD-style, and hybrid distillation modes—equipped with built-in estimators including sampled-token, Top- K K , full-vocabulary, and Jensen–Shannon Divergence (JSD) KL strategies. • Systemic Train–Inference Consistency: To prevent off-policy drift, LoongSage treats train–inference consistency as a systematically enforced property. It deploys a defense-in-depth architecture combining Deterministic Source Alignment (e.g., MoE routing replay), selective precision pinning for critical layers, and algorithmic residual corrections (including TIS, M2PO, and OPSM; detailed in Section 4.5 ) to guarantee the optimization plane reliably tracks the sampling distribution. • Lightweight, Usable, and Highly Extensible: By maintaining a strict zero-fork dependency on its backend engines, the lightweight core transparently inherits upstream optimizations and auto-expands its model library without tedious framework adaptations. Additionally, a highly extensible plugin system exposes ten core extension points—spanning agents, reward models, and scheduling strategies. This enables configuration-driven hot-plugging of new algorithms, allowing rapid iteration without modifying the framework’s main trunk. 2 Related Work 2.1 The Evolution of LLM Post-Training Compositional Paradigms. Modern LLM post-training is converging toward a compositional pipeline rather than a single optimization objective. Supervised fine-tuning establishes base capabilities and response formats, after which reinforcement learning optimizes the policy against a reward signal. Building on knowledge distillation ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) , on-policy distillation then adds a denser supervision channel, transferring the output distributions of one or more teachers onto the student’s own rollouts ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . These stages differ in where supervision originates and in whether generation happens inside the training loop, yet they increasingly share the same training and inference infrastructure. Frameworks therefore need to compose objectives and data flows without forcing every new method into a separate execution stack. From RLHF to RLVR. Reinforcement learning entered LLM post-training as RLHF, which fits a reward model to preference comparisons and optimizes the policy with PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ) . Later work then moved in two directions, one of which removes online RL altogether by reparameterizing the preference objective, as DPO does ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) . The other retains online RL but replaces the learned reward model with a programmatic checker, which in turn simplifies the algorithms themselves. GRPO drops the value network in favor of group-relative advantages ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , and DAPO combines decoupled clipping, dynamic sampling, and token-level loss aggregation for large-scale RLVR ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . The transition also moves the systems cost from reward-model and reference-policy management toward rollout generation, program execution, sample filtering, and reliable aggregation of completed outcomes. Agentic RL. As models are deployed in more complex settings, RL is shifting toward agentic tasks with multi-turn interaction and external environments, building on early evidence that LLMs can be taught to invoke tools and APIs, whether by in-context prompting or by fine-tuning ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Schick et al., 2023 ; Qin et al., 2024 ) . An agentic reward evaluates whether a task was completed rather than whether a single response was correct, so producing it depends on tool use and sandboxed execution against a live environment ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) . Unlike single-turn generation, the resulting trajectory contains intermediate observations, actions, and tool results whose contribution to the final outcome may be delayed. A practical training system must therefore preserve the generated sequence and its metadata across multiple turns, tolerate heavy-tailed episode lengths and external-environment failures, and manage the sandbox lifecycle ( Luo et al., 2025 ) . 2.2 Distributed Training and Inference Systems Parallelism and Distributed Training. Large-model training combines data, tensor, pipeline, and expert parallelism to overcome single-GPU limits, and Megatron-LM provides optimized implementations of these strategies ( Shoeybi et al., 2019 ) . DeepSpeed and ZeRO instead reduce memory use by partitioning optimizer states, gradients, and parameters ( Rasley et al., 2020 ; Rajbhandari et al., 2020 ) . On top of these placement decisions, RL post-training adds a further requirement, because the inference side must generate rollouts concurrently or alternately with the distributed training side. Resource placement and the synchronization relation between the two sides therefore become part of the framework design. Orchestration and Inference Engines. Ray manages heterogeneous pipeline components across a cluster ( Moritz et al., 2018 ) , while rollout generation relies on dedicated serving engines. vLLM improves throughput through continuous batching and PagedAttention ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) , and SGLang targets multi-turn and structured LLM programs ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) . Because rollout requests have variable lengths and may invoke tools whereas training requires tightly synchronized collective computation, orchestration must coordinate two distinct lifecycles and resource layouts rather than treating inference as a simple preprocessing step. 2.3 RL Frameworks Foundational RL Frameworks. OpenRLHF ( Hu et al., 2025 ) established an accessible combination of distributed training and high-throughput inference. NeMo-Aligner ( Shen et al., 2024 ) targets Megatron-based scale, TRL ( von Werra et al., 2020 ) emphasizes Hugging Face usability, verl ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) uses a controller-centered HybridFlow model, and slime ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) narrows the dependency surface by pairing Megatron-LM with SGLang. Together these systems span accessibility, ecosystem integration, large-scale backend support, expressive control flow, and a deliberately small dependency surface. Agentic workloads, however, further require explicit support for trajectory structure, resource sharing, and the boundary between rollout and optimization. Asynchronous Execution and Rollout Management. AReaL ( Fu et al., 2026 ) makes asynchronous generation and training the default and mitigates long-tail latency by buffering unfinished trajectories for later continuation, which improves utilization at the cost of trajectory staleness. Agent-Lightning ( Luo et al., 2025 ) instead disaggregates the agent from the trainer, while agent frameworks and benchmarks such as SWE-agent ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , OpenHands ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , WebArena ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) , and OSWorld ( Xie et al., 2024 ) motivate support for long-horizon interaction and persistent state. These directions expose a central trade-off in which decoupling improves utilization and accommodates long-running interactions while also increasing coordination complexity and the possibility that training consumes data produced by older policy versions. A framework should therefore expose this trade-off as a configurable policy rather than a fixed behavior, and keep one interface for trajectories, weight transfer, and training regardless of the execution mode. 3 The LoongSage Framework This section describes the system architecture of LoongSage and the orchestration of its principal components within an agentic RL training pipeline. By establishing strict boundaries across orchestration, data representation, and backend integration, the framework accommodates both synchronous and fully asynchronous execution within a unified architecture. Figure 1 situates LoongSage against the most closely related systems across four structural axes: training and inference backends, agent integration methodology, support for multi-teacher distillation, and execution asynchrony. Rather than pursuing broad backend agnosticism or unrestricted scheduling, LoongSage commits to an optimized pairing of specific engines and bounded asynchronous execution. This focus lets the framework address the central challenges of agentic workloads: ensuring the fidelity of trajectories fed to the optimizer, orchestrating multi-teacher distillation at scale, and maintaining observability over the train–inference gap (detailed in Section 4.5 ). Figure 1: Positioning of LoongSage relative to closely related systems. Each entry is compiled from the publicly available documentation of the corresponding project at the time of writing. A dash indicates a capability that is not documented, rather than one that cannot be realized within the system. 3.1 Design Trade-offs The architectural design of LoongSage is guided by three core principles, aimed at ensuring that long-running agentic RL training remains transparent, deterministic, and diagnosable in the event of systemic failures. One controller, many workers. All system orchestration is centralized within a single controller process, where the Trainer acts as the sole state machine dictating every phase transition. GPU-resident components operate as Ray actors, exposing coarse-grained control methods and returning ObjectRef s. Crucially, the controller executes no forward passes and holds no model parameters, guaranteeing that the global state of a long-running distributed job can be fully inspected from this single process. Control signals are kept intentionally coarse to amortize the overhead of Ray serialization and remote procedure calls (RPCs). Token-level internal boundaries. The internal interface between the sampling and optimization planes operates strictly at the token level—exchanging token sequences coupled with their respective log-probabilities, loss masks, and weight versions. Human-readable text exists only at the outermost protocol edge where the agent interacts. This abstraction eliminates re-tokenization discrepancies, a major source of implicit train–inference divergence (Section 4.1 ). Thin trunk with named seams. LoongSage builds natively upon Megatron-Core, Megatron-Bridge, and SGLang without introducing cumbersome abstraction layers for alternative backends. To maximize extensibility, algorithmic components—such as agents, reward models, policy losses, and asynchronous scheduling strategies—are exposed via named registry entries (seams) rather than through rigid subclassing of a monolithic framework class. This approach yields a modular architecture, enabling researchers to substitute custom logic through configuration files alone without altering the framework’s core. 3.2 System Organization LoongSage structurally decomposes the RL pipeline into seven interacting planes: control, sampling, training, algorithm, data, transfer, and resource. These planes communicate exclusively via well-defined data objects and control interfaces, preserving the readability of the core logic while allowing targeted functionality to be added through configuration. The control plane is anchored by the Trainer , which orchestrates the state transitions for each algorithmic step. Dedicated lifecycle managers— TrainManager , RolloutManager , and TeacherManager —oversee the training, inference, and teacher worker pools, respectively. The RolloutSampler maps step-level data requirements into batched sampling tasks. To prevent tangled dependencies, these managers never invoke one another directly. Instead, the Trainer sequences them according to the current training phase, cleanly isolating orchestration logic from the compute backends and enabling independent backend evolution. Figure 2: Overall system architecture of LoongSage. As illustrated in Figure 2 , the sampling plane is governed by AgentFlow, which translates unstructured multi-turn agent interactions into trainable trajectories. By operating the agent externally, LoongSage embraces the disaggregated design philosophy advocated by Agent-Lightning. AgentFlow’s token-level alignment and multi-agent support are detailed in Section 4.1 . The training plane wraps the Megatron-based worker pool that executes the forward, backward, and optimizer passes over admitted trajectories. The algorithm plane exposes registries for advantage estimation ( Schulman et al., 2015 ) , policy losses, and KL divergence constraints, and additionally provides configurable importance-sampling corrections ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) and off-policy sequence masking ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) . The data plane governs Multi-Data-Source Mixed Training , managing stateful data loading, admission filtering, and data-parallel partitioning. It enables the independent configuration of agents, rewards, and sampling parameters per source, while strictly maintaining global data mixture proportions invariant across all ranks and mini-batches. The transfer plane, instantiated as TransferMesh (Section 4.3 ), manages topology-aware weight synchronization. Finally, the resource plane orchestrates cluster allocations via Ray placement groups and GPU bundles. 3.3 Training Flow and Placement Under the default synchronous execution mode, a training step proceeds through four distinct stages. During the sampling stage , the RolloutSampler fetches prompt groups from various data sources and dispatches sampling tasks. In the admission stage , completed trajectories are grouped and evaluated by a data filter. Because rejections occur post-generation, the sampler proactively over-samples a configurable buffer per data source, refilling rejected slots within a bounded budget and enforcing step-level timeouts for stalled requests. During the aggregation stage , the controller aligns admitted trajectories with the active policy version and data-parallel layout, while teacher workers compute necessary distillation signals. Finally, in the update stage , training workers execute the forward, backward, and optimizer passes, concluding with the transfer of updated parameters back to the inference engine for the subsequent rollout. The fully asynchronous mode eliminates this strict synchronization barrier, enabling the sampling and optimization engines to make concurrent progress via a decoupled train–rollout buffer. The buffering, freshness constraints, and recovery mechanics of this mode are detailed in Section 4.2 . Execution coupling and resource placement are treated as orthogonal architectural axes (Figure 3 ). Colocated placement time-multiplexes device memory so that both engines and the weight-update phase fit on the same GPUs, whereas disaggregated placement dedicates disjoint hardware pools to each engine. Both placement strategies share an identical underlying scheduler, controller, AgentFlow paradigm, and weight-transfer interface, allowing deployments to scale flexibly based on model size and cluster topology. Among the four possible combinations of these two axes, three are structurally supported. Fully asynchronous execution inherently conflicts with colocation, as overlapping rollout and training mandates simultaneous memory residency for both engines. Figure 3: The two orthogonal configuration axes behind LoongSage’s operational modes, their trade-offs, and the combination that the framework does not support. 4 Key Features This section details the principal mechanisms underpinning LoongSage’s agentic RL pipeline. We focus on how the framework guarantees trajectory fidelity across diverse agent topologies, orchestrates multi-teacher supervision, seamlessly overlaps rollout with optimization, executes topology-aware weight transfers, and exposes highly extensible API boundaries. 4.1 Seamless Integration of Any Agent LoongSage integrates arbitrary agents with zero intrusion into their internal logic. Agents interact with the framework exclusively via a router URL exposing the standard OpenAI Chat Completions API, remaining entirely agnostic to the underlying tokenization, trajectory storage, and sandbox lifecycles. AgentFlow operates as the sampling plane enabling this abstraction—mediating among agents, the inference engine, and the training data pipeline to deterministically convert multi-turn interactions into replayable RL trajectories, as illustrated in Figure 4 . Figure 4: The AgentFlow request path. The Router intercepts each Chat Completions request, tokenizes the turn, dispatches it to SGLang’s /generate , and records the returned tokens per turn in the TrajectoryStore . Supported agents fall into two structurally distinct categories. A white-box agent implements its interaction loop internally within LoongSage, directly controlling tool invocations and LLM requests. Consequently, its trajectory forms a linear, append-only sequence of prompts, responses, tool execution results, and termination signals. Conversely, a black-box agent executes as an opaque binary or script within an isolated sandbox. Here, the framework manages the entry point and intercepts outgoing requests, yielding complex, non-linear trajectories that require a tree-structured storage backend. The current repository natively supports white-box GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , and Mini-SWE agents, alongside a black-box OpenCode agent ( OpenCode Contributors, 2025 ) . As depicted in Figure 5 , AgentFlow represents each trajectory as a flattened, contiguous token array, tightly coupled with position-aligned arrays for loss masks, rollout log-probabilities, weight versions, routed experts, and token-level rewards. To minimize memory overhead, a Segment struct tracks token and response spans, while a Triplet struct records individual model interactions using index ranges rather than duplicating token data. Tool observations are injected into the response space with a zeroed loss mask, placeholder log-probabilities, and an invalid ( − 1 -1 ) weight version. A mutated weight version explicitly flags a turn interrupted by an asynchronous model update. Finally, only the terminal position encodes the scalar task reward R R , ensuring all sampling statistics for generated tokens remain intact throughout the pipeline. Figure 5: Data representation under TITO: a single flattened token array with its position-aligned response-space arrays, referenced by Segment and Triplet indices rather than copied. Token-In, Token-Out (TITO). A core mechanism of AgentFlow is storing the exact tokens consumed and generated by the inference engine, deliberately avoiding the practice of re-tokenizing textual messages prior to training. Such re-tokenization often introduces compounding discrepancies between the sampled and trained sequences due to whitespace handling, special tokens, reasoning markers, or tool-call serialization. Under TITO, high-level textual requests and responses are mapped transparently to their internal token representations at the framework’s outermost boundary, ensuring the sampled and trained sequences remain identical. Consequently, completed trajectories can be annotated with validity, scalar, or fine-grained rewards without corrupting the original sampling record. For white-box agents, AgentFlow reuses established token prefixes as conversational histories expand. For black-box agents, it dynamically reconstructs mutated context segments while preserving their topological relationships. Should a long-horizon trajectory be interrupted, its sandbox state can also be preserved and reused, preventing the loss of intermediate file edits or process states. The framework’s sandbox interface provides native Kubernetes and Docker backends. Thus, agents requiring shell execution are securely isolated within ephemeral pods or containers whose lifecycles are strictly bound to the trajectory. Compaction and Multi-Agent Control. State-of-the-art black-box agents (e.g., OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex) natively embed automatic context compaction and multi-agent collaboration mechanisms. These behaviors inherently rewrite or fork the conversation history, violating the standard linear Markov Decision Process (MDP) assumption. Consequently, a naive linear trajectory store would immediately fail prefix matching upon context compaction or subtask delegation. To overcome this, AgentFlow records every trajectory as a directed tree of segments (Figure 6 ). Tree edges are defined by segment_id and parent_segment_id pointers, while an origin tag explicitly categorizes each node as a mainline start ( root ), a compaction-induced continuation ( compact ), or a spawned subtask ( subagent ). Crucially, only mainline segments are designated as trainable, earning the right to populate the flat token, loss-mask, and log-probability arrays depicted in Figure 5 . If a prefix mismatch occurs and the request is not explicitly a collab_spawn , the trajectory opens a new mainline branch to re-tokenize the compacted context. Conversely, a collab_spawn request forks a subagent segment one level deeper in the hierarchy. Because multi-agent credit assignment remains an open research problem, LoongSage currently treats subagent segments as non-trainable placeholders that merely track their tree position ( token_start = token_end ). This architectural decision prevents premature commitment to a flawed reward decomposition while preserving a robust extension point for future multi-agent RL capabilities. Figure 6: AgentFlow stores a black-box trajectory as a tree of segments: trainable mainline segments ( origin=root or compact ) own the flat token arrays, while a collab_spawn request forks a non-trainable subagent placeholder ( origin=subagent ). Stateful Routing and Protocol Isolation. This abstraction is enforced via a strict protocol boundary. Upstream parser middleware translates incoming JSON messages into raw token IDs, and symmetrically converts generated token distributions back into standard chat completions. To maximize inference throughput, the routing layer utilizes session affinity, pinning all requests from a single trajectory to a specific inference worker. This guarantees KV-cache and prefix reuse across multiple turns, falling back to the least-loaded worker only if the pinned node becomes unresponsive or reaches capacity. Black-box agents utilizing proprietary APIs (i.e., those deviating from /v1/chat/completions ) are bridged into the unified tree store via protocol adapters (Figure 7 ). For instance, Codex ( /v1/responses ) and Claude Code ( /v1/messages ) each map to a dedicated adapter that normalizes their wire formats into LoongSage’s internal message and tool schemas, keeping the downstream parser, tokenizer, and trajectory storage decoupled from upstream API idiosyncrasies. Support for these proprietary APIs is under active development (Appendix B ). Recent iterations of Claude Code expose explicit metadata fields for subagent requests, enabling the adapter to flag subagent spawns within the tree structure. Figure 7: The protocol adapter normalizes each agent’s wire format into one internal request: OpenCode over Chat Completions, Codex over OpenAI Responses, and Claude Code over Anthropic Messages. A single parser, tokenizer, and SGLang path then serve all of them. 4.2 Staleness-Bounded Fully Asynchronous Training In fully asynchronous mode, rollout freshness is no longer implicitly guaranteed by a synchronized schedule. Explicit staleness control thus becomes mandatory when overlapping the training and inference engines to eliminate idle time and repeated initialization overhead. Figure 8 illustrates the resulting decoupled pipeline. Figure 8: The fully asynchronous pipeline’s control points reduce to two gates—a dispatch gate and a collection gate. Table 1 lists the mathematical bounds each registered policy places on them. This producer-consumer architecture aligns with contemporary asynchronous RL systems ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Sheng et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; MiniMax, 2026 ) . The rollout engine generates trajectories, a collector aggregates the completed ones into training groups, and the training engine consumes them from a shared buffer. Conceptually, this decoupling introduces only two degrees of freedom for data ingestion: determining how many new rollouts to dispatch, and deciding which completed groups are eligible for training. All underlying logic transparently reuses the synchronous-mode implementation. The agents, trajectory representations, and topology-aware weight transfers remain completely unchanged, ensuring the two engines only synchronize at deterministic weight-update boundaries. Bounding Staleness. In a fully asynchronous pipeline, maximizing hardware utilization inherently trades off data freshness. If the inference engine significantly outpaces the trainer, the buffer accumulates trajectories generated by outdated policy weights, severely exacerbating off-policy drift. Conversely, if the framework enforces excessively tight synchronization to prevent this drift, the trainer inevitably starves while waiting for new rollouts, negating the throughput benefits of asynchrony. To systematically navigate this throughput–staleness Pareto frontier, LoongSage introduces three sliding-window scheduling policies. These policies act as dynamic constraints on the dispatch and collection gates, strictly bounding the maximum allowable version gap between the generation policy and the optimization policy. Furthermore, because LoongSage attributes metrics exclusively to the data actually consumed during an optimization step, the systemic impact of each policy on off-policy divergence remains fully transparent and directly observable in the training logs. Consequently, scheduling is abstracted as a configuration-driven registry seam rather than deeply nested branching logic. Notably, in the staleness column, some guarantees hold by strict mathematical construction, whereas others materialize implicitly once uncollected groups accumulate at the collection gate. no-window (Figure 9 a) dispatches a new group the moment an active slot frees up. Its only capacity limit exists to prevent host memory exhaustion rather than to bound off-policy drift. Because a completed group immediately yields its slot, short requests finish and enter the training phase in rapid succession. Meanwhile, a computationally heavy, long-horizon request may be interrupted by multiple asynchronous weight updates without bound. This inherently introduces a severe length-biased sampling pathology, skewing the training distribution toward shorter trajectories. window-gated (Figure 9 b) imposes a hard gate, refusing to dispatch any task whose sequence number exceeds the oldest in-flight one by more than the window W = B ⁡ ( 1 + S ) W=B(1+S) . The window advances only when the oldest group completes. While this strictly bounds staleness to ≤ S \leq S steps, it risks severe pipeline under-utilization due to head-of-line blocking from long-tail requests. The worst-case scenario occurs when the entire training pipeline stalls, waiting idly for a single straggler to clear the window. In practice, however, the window typically advances fluidly as subsequent requests finish ahead of the straggler. windowed-fifo (Figure 9 c) adopts its nomenclature and collection heuristic from Forge. It retains the aggressive capacity-based dispatch rule without generation bounds but restricts collection: a completed group is only ingested if it falls within one batch of the oldest in-flight sequence number. Groups completing too far ahead are discarded and never trained. This bounds off-policy drift once uncollected groups accumulate and critically enforces an ordering constraint that mitigates the aforementioned short-trajectory bias (quantified against no-window in Section 5.3 ). The collection window is fixed at one batch. A smaller window would artificially constrain ordering within a single step, while a significantly larger one would simply degenerate into no-window . The underlying buffer operates as a priority queue keyed by dataset order, ensuring the training sequence mirrors synchronous mode as closely as physical completion times permit. As training and inference pipelines are increasingly decoupled, weight synchronization emerges as the primary coordination bottleneck, often dominating the per-step overhead for massive-scale models. TransferMesh mitigates this by dynamically discovering the physical placement of participating actors during channel initialization and routing traffic across the most efficient hardware-level topology. Figure 10 depicts this topology-aware routing architecture. Figure 10: TransferMesh packs the named tensor stream into one contiguous memory bucket described by a single metadata frame, then dynamically selects a transport protocol per receiver based on device topology: utilizing a zero-copy CUDA IPC handle for colocated engines and an NCCL broadcast for remote receivers. At its core, TransferMesh abstracts a global weight update as a named tensor stream . When the sender yields parameters, the transfer layer coalesces them into contiguous memory buckets, recording metadata—tensor name, shape, data type, and byte offsets—into a separate layout descriptor. Receivers fetch this lightweight descriptor first, allowing them to reconstruct the tensor stream for the inference engine. This decouples the two engines’ internal memory layouts and amortizes the high latency and kernel-launch overheads of point-to-point transfers of fragmented, fine-grained tensors. The underlying transport dynamically adapts to the discovered hardware topology. When training and inference processes are colocated on the same physical device, TransferMesh exchanges a CUDA Inter-Process Communication (IPC) handle pointing to the sender’s memory bucket. This achieves zero-copy parameter sharing, bypassing redundant VRAM allocations and PCIe/NVLink traversals. For remote receivers, the bulk payload is broadcast via an optimized NCCL collective. All metadata and IPC handles are transmitted out-of-band via a lightweight Gloo channel, letting receivers pre-allocate the required device buffers and reconstruct parameters with their original shapes and precisions before the bulk transfer begins. To guarantee system stability, TransferMesh operates on an orthogonal communication context. This structural isolation ensures the weight-transfer fabric never collides or deadlocks with the backend engines’ internal data-parallel or tensor-parallel collective operations. While the transfer protocol itself is strictly backend-agnostic at the tensor-stream boundary, the currently shipped adapters natively interface with Megatron’s parameter export and SGLang’s weight-loading routines. Consequently, migrating to an alternative training or inference backend reduces entirely to implementing a localized memory-layout adapter, without modifying the underlying synchronization infrastructure. 4.4 Full-Vocabulary Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation On-policy distillation trains a student model on its self-generated rollouts while leveraging one or more teacher models for dense, token-level distributional supervision. Any systemic deviation skews the importance-sampling ratio, silently degrading the optimization process into an unstable off-policy regime. LoongSage treats this consistency not merely as an algorithmic assumption, but as a continuously observable and localizable systemic property. Potential sources of divergence span multiple layers: textual re-tokenization mismatches, arithmetic precision truncation, non-equivalent fused kernels ( Dao et al., 2022 ) , mismatched quantization schemes between engines, non-deterministic discrete decisions (e.g., Mixture-of-Experts routing), and minor variances in parallel reduction or padding. To counteract this drift, the framework implements a defense-in-depth strategy categorized into source alignment, precision anchoring, and residual correction (summarized in Figure 13 ). Figure 13: Train–inference consistency is handled in three groups: source alignment guarantees the trained sequence mathematically matches the sampled sequence, long-context and precision settings anchor numerical stability, and residual corrections continuously bound the remaining gap. Deterministic Source Alignment and Routing Replay. As established in Section 4.1 , TITO removes re-tokenization discrepancies at the input boundary. For Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures ( Fedus et al., 2022 ; Jiang et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) , LoongSage integrates Rollout Routing Replay (R3) ( Ma et al., 2025 ) . Rather than allowing microscopic logit perturbations to randomly flip computation paths during training, R3 explicitly records the exact experts selected by the inference engine for every token across every MoE layer. The framework then deterministically replays this exact routing tensor during the training forward pass. While the router weights continue to receive gradients normally, the structural computation path remains rigidly locked to the sampled trajectory. This replay mechanism remains mathematically robust even under partial rollout, as a trajectory spanning multiple weight versions safely replays the historical routing context utilized during its original generation. Context Parallelism and Selective Precision Pinning. To support the extended trajectories inherent to agentic tasks without introducing padding artifacts or breaking numerical determinism, sequences are tightly packed into THD format, and contexts are partitioned via contiguous-chunk Context Parallelism (CP) ( Liu et al., 2024 ) —under which MoE routing replay remains strictly valid. While the bulk of the model’s compute operates in BF16, LoongSage introduces Selective Precision Pinning , allowing developers to anchor highly sensitive parameters to FP32 in both memory storage and layer-wise computation. Production recipes specifically apply this to the output layer (LM Head). Because reduced-precision rounding at the output layer sharply distorts softmax log-probabilities—historically the dominant source of numerical drift in dense models—pinning it effectively neutralizes a primary train–inference gap, trading a marginal memory and compute overhead for critical numerical stability. Algorithmic Residual Correction and Monitoring. Because source alignment cannot fully eliminate hardware-level kernel discrepancies or the weight-version staleness inherent to asynchronous execution, the algorithm plane provisions a spectrum of residual defenses spanning both token and sequence granularities. At the fine-grained token level, LoongSage natively supports Truncated Importance Sampling (TIS) ( Ionides, 2008 ; Yao et al., 2025 ) and Masked Importance Sampling (MIS). These methods reweight the step-wise loss using the ratio π train / π rollout \pi_{\text{train}}/\pi_{\text{rollout}} —the discrepancy between the training engine’s recomputed probabilities and the inference engine’s sampling probabilities—while clipping or bounding out-of-range values. To mitigate compounded drift over long-horizon tasks, the framework elevates these defenses via explicit sequence-level corrections, which recalibrate the objective based on the cumulative trajectory ratio. Furthermore, it integrates advanced sequence-level filtering mechanisms like Second-Moment Trust Policy Optimization (M2PO) and Off-Policy Sequence Masking (OPSM), which discard or mask extreme trajectory outliers to prevent pathological samples from dominating a gradient update. An alternative execution mode treats π rollout \pi_{\text{rollout}} as the definitive behavior policy, implicitly absorbing the gap and bypassing reference log-probability recomputation—an optimization that is structurally mutually exclusive with TIS, MIS, and M2PO. Regardless of the chosen configuration, the framework continuously monitors the K3 KL divergence estimate, the token-clipping ratio, and weight-version staleness spans. While algorithmic clipping and OPSM act as safeguards against off-policy drift, LoongSage treats aligning critical kernels, replaying discrete MoE decisions, and pinning precision on critical paths as the primary systemic remedies. 4.6 Lightweight, Usable, and Highly Extensible Beyond its distributed mechanics, LoongSage is engineered to minimize technical debt and cognitive load for researchers. After excluding blank lines, comments, and tests, the framework comprises a minimalist core of roughly 14,000 lines of Python. Minimalist Core and Zero-Fork Integration. The architectural boundaries within LoongSage are designed by applying strict interface segregation. A prime example is TransferMesh (Section 4.3 ): the controller issues a single channel descriptor to both sides, completely shielding the training and inference engines from the underlying transport and channel-rebuild complexities. Any transient backend fixes are maintained as isolated, hot-applied patches that can be cleanly deprecated once resolved upstream. By relying exclusively on these foundational libraries alongside Ray and Hydra, the framework transparently inherits all upstream distributed optimizations and automatically expands its supported model library in tandem with the Megatron-Bridge ecosystem. Under its single-controller orchestration model, LoongSage unifies arbitrary agent interactions, multi-turn trajectory materialization, multi-teacher distillation, and distributed policy optimization into a cohesive, modular architecture. Built upon this foundation, the framework delivers six architectural contributions: (1) zero-intrusion TITO integration for diverse white- and black-box agent topologies; (2) staleness-bounded, fully asynchronous pipeline execution; (3) topology-aware TransferMesh weight synchronization; (4) memory-multiplexed, full-vocabulary multi-teacher distillation; (5) systemic train–inference consistency maintained by design; and (6) a lightweight, zero-fork core exposing a configuration-driven plugin system. Collectively, these mechanisms address the engineering bottlenecks imposed by long-horizon multi-turn rollouts, severe heavy-tail latency, and large-scale distributed resource coordination. Extensive empirical evaluations spanning mathematical reasoning, complex software engineering, black-box coding agents, and multi-teacher distillation validate that LoongSage drives agentic training while strictly bounding train–inference divergence and minimizing systemic overhead. Looking ahead, our roadmap focuses on evolving LoongSage into a comprehensive post-training ecosystem. To further optimize memory utilization at scale, we will introduce cross-node distributed storage for multi-teacher weights and native low-precision training primitives. Algorithmically, we intend to broaden the framework’s unified pipeline to encompass Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), alongside native support for omni-modal architectures. We hope LoongSage provides the open-source and academic communities with a highly usable, extensible foundation, accelerating future breakthroughs in large-scale agentic AI systems. Appendix B Operational Notes and Limitations Stabilizing the DeepSeek-V4-Flash SWE training recipe surfaced a range of systemic failures that are invisible at the algorithmic level, yet determine whether a large-scale distributed job can reach completion. We categorize these observations to aid future infrastructure developers: Hard Systemic Failures. These faults abruptly halt execution, manifesting through explicit crash signals or out-of-memory (OOM) triggers. Examples encountered during scale-up include: numerical instability (NaNs) in early Megatron-Core versions when shared-expert overlap was enabled; SGLang exhausting device VRAM specifically during topology weight updates; a cuDNN DSA kernel triggering illegal memory corruption; and a CuTe launch cache silently leaking after several hundred steps. Furthermore, an FP32 output-layer pinning unexpectedly broke Megatron’s checkpoint saver, while the CPU optimizer exhausted host memory and crashed. At the framework orchestration level, repeated JIT operator recompilation under dynamic batching induced steady host RAM bloating, and a memory-saver hook conflict between SGLang and Megatron-Core deterministically crashed the inference engine upon CUDA-graph capture. Silent Structural and Arithmetic Corruptions. More subtly, these anomalies yield no explicit crash signals, allowing training to proceed while corrupting the RL objective. For instance, a PDL dependency anomaly within a FlashInfer CuTe-DSL rmsnorm kernel introduced an asynchronous timing hazard, silently perturbing normalization statistics and inflating the measured train–inference gap. In another instance, a parameter had identical tensor shapes across both engines but used different memory layouts, causing weight updates to complete without error yet populate the tensor with corrupted data. Similarly, an incorrectly implemented clamp in the shared-expert activation quietly widened the distribution gap. Because such defects fail silently, the policy can degrade for extended periods while conventional metrics appear normal—underscoring the necessity of continuously monitoring the sampling–training gap rather than verifying it only at bring-up. These real-world challenges highlight a key realization for the agentic RL era: reinforcement learning acts as a strong amplifier for software and hardware coupling . Minute variances in operator implementations, non-deterministic CUDA rounding, reduction-order variance in collectives, and dynamic batch-size adjustments are fed back into the policy via the reward signal. Consequently, hyperparameters alone are insufficient to fully describe a reproducible RL recipe . The configurations shipped with LoongSage encode the resolutions to these systemic hazards, making them production-validated deployment blueprints rather than mere algorithmic settings. Current Architectural Boundaries and Roadmap. Several boundaries of the current implementation define our immediate developmental roadmap. First, the protocol adapters (Section 4.1 ) for black-box agents utilizing proprietary APIs (deviating from /v1/chat/completions ) are actively being finalized. Second, for certain black-box agents, the framework’s parser cannot yet deterministically classify whether a new branch stems from context compaction or a spawned subtask, necessitating that subtask segments temporarily remain non-trainable placeholders. Third, cross-node memory pooling for teacher weights—designed to utilize idle host RAM on training and rollout nodes as a global distributed weight cache—currently exists as a defined interface awaiting backend implementation. Fourth, the fully asynchronous mode does not yet match the synchronous path’s generality regarding heterogeneous multi-data-source routing and multi-agent topologies, and its asynchronous metric aggregation requires finer precision tuning. Taken together, these boundaries feed directly into the broader roadmap outlined in Section 6 , which additionally targets prefill–decode disaggregation for inference to relieve the operational bottlenecks discussed above. Rather than isolated engineering caveats, we regard these limitations as concrete, prioritized extension points: each is scoped against a stable interface, so closing it broadens the framework’s coverage without perturbing the orchestration core. We further anticipate that the systemic hazards catalogued here will recur in new guises as models and backends evolve, and the corresponding resolutions will continue to be folded into the shipped recipes. By documenting both the failures and their fixes in the open, we aim to spare the community the recurring cost of rediscovering them and to invite contributions that harden agentic RL infrastructure at scale.
